Between Tradition and Transformation: ATU Classification and Lüthian Formal Analysis of Sophia de Mello Breyner Andresen’s The Girl from the Sea and Other Stories
abstract: Abstract Sophia de Mello Breyner Andresen is among the most celebrated of Portuguese poets, yet the eight literary fairy tales gathered in English as The Girl from the Sea and Other Stories (2020), first published separately in Portuguese from 1958 onwards, have rarely been read for their form. This essay reads the collection, together with the separately published Saga , as Kunstmärchen, fairy tales composed by a named author who deliberately reworks an inherited tradition. Bringing two frameworks to bear, the Aarne-Thompson-Uther (ATU) index of international tale types and Max Lüthi’s account of the formal characteristics of the European fairy tale, we argue that Andresen’s tales are at once deeply traditional and quietly transformative. Read by type, several of the tale-type attributions the collection might seem to invite prove untenable on close reading and are revised here; read by form, the tales display a consistent fairy-tale poetics whose abstract style is realised through Andresen’s distinctive language of stone, glass and metal. “Here Lies a Bird that is Dead”: Children’s Funeral Games in Contemporary Picturebooks
abstract: Abstract This article examines a contemplative yet underexplored topic, children’s playful funerals in death-themed picturebooks. Taking Margaret Wise Brown’s The Dead Bird as a foundational case, this work compares a group of picturebooks sharing a similar thematic pattern: children finding a dead animal by accident, organising funerals for the animal and then returning to play. Drawing on Victor Turner’s theory of ritual process and performance studies, these activities, in between childly games and formal funeral practices, cannot be simply read as children’s responses to loss and grief. Through flexibly modifying the spatial organisation of ritual sites and children’s bodily engagement with the material surroundings, selected picturebooks invite both characters and young readers to negotiate their agency and identities as members of a living community. Multiple nuances over time are also observed during the diachronic reading, reflecting the ever-changing implications of death in children’s literature. title: Performing Church in Dystopia
abstract: Abstract Suzanne Collins’s books about the Hunger Games lack references to religious beliefs or practices. However, in this article I argue that the resistance to oppression in the books can be read theologically, starting from an understanding of the church as a visible social body. Building on the political and liturgical theology of William T. Cavanaugh, I discuss how the scattering effects of torture are challenged in The Hunger Games . I focus on how bodily resistance to the practices of torture is described in Collins’s books and connect this to Cavanaugh’s theology about community, individuality, and the idea of ritual practices as resistance. Finally, I discuss how the anti-liturgy of torture is challenged when the performance of social bodies introduces elements of linearity in the repetitive cycle of isolating rituals. The Hunger Games is often read as an individualistic narrative about an individualistic heroine. Reading it in dialogue with Cavanaugh sheds light on how the formation of a social body is a significant part of Katniss’s resistance, both toward the Capitol and later toward the rebels from District 13.

title: Learning Values Through Stories: The Impact of Narrative-Based Activities on Social and Civic Development in Early Childhood Education
abstract: Abstract The pedagogical efficacy of children’s stories within the classroom is fundamentally contingent upon critical teacher mediation, thereby transcending the traditional perspective that may regard them merely as a source of entertainment. The primary objective of this research is to analyse the impact of stories focused on social and civic values on a group of four- to five-year-old children. To achieve this, we employed a qualitative methodology and data collection techniques, such as the teacher’s reflective diary (documenting each session), semi-structured interviews with two participating teachers, unfinished stories created by the lead teacher to encourage co-construction, transcripts of children’s responses to ethical dilemmas during assemblies, and creative productions such as drawings and collaboratively composed story endings. The findings revealed that even an unhappy story can provoke meaningful reflection, encourage the proposal of alternatives, and foster prosocial attitudes and emotional well-being in children. Analyzing Representations of Asian American Characters and Stories on the Book Covers of Newbery, Caldecott, and Printz Award-Winning Children’s and Youth Literature
abstract: Abstract This study examined representations of Asian American characters and their stories as depicted on the covers of 18 American Library Association award-winning books for children and young adults published between 2017 and 2025. The awards focused on were the John Newbery Medal, the Randolph Caldecott Medal, and the Michael L. Printz Award. Both the visual and verbal aspects of the covers were analyzed. This study was grounded in Asian critical race theory and also drew from scholarship focused on Asian American children’s literature, literary awards, and critical visual analysis. This multimodal content analysis revealed five degrees of Asian American representation, ranging from overt visual and linguistic representation to blurry or unshown depictions of Asian American identities. Transnational border crossings were also visible within the data corpus, often indexed by the language included on the book covers but also shown through cover visuals. This study contributes to conversations about diverse, authentic representation in children’s literature and draws attention to book covers as important opportunities for peritextual literary analysis. title: Bishop’s Categories 40 Years on: Reclaiming and Sustaining Story and Culture Authors
abstract: Abstract Bishop’s foundational framework for analysing multicultural children’s literature has provided essential tools for understanding cultural representation for almost 40 years. However, the evolution of First Nations children’s literature and the increased Indigenous control over publishing and storytelling suggest Bishop’s original three categories may not fully capture the complexity of contemporary Indigenous storytelling. This study reports on a comprehensive analysis of 750 books by and about Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, employing yarning methodology and Indigenous research approaches to examine patterns of cultural representation across historical periods. Whilst Bishop’s categories remain relevant, two additional categories emerged: Culturally Sustaining and Cultural Storytellers. Culturally Sustaining stories encompass literature that actively explores cultural continuity, intergenerational knowledge transmission, and connection to Country. The Cultural Storytellers category captures works by First Nations authors reclaiming narrative authority to tell universal stories naturally infused with cultural knowledge. The Tapestry of Care in Good Night, Mr. Tom: Reciprocity, Remembrance, and Resilience
abstract: Abstract This study analyzes Good Night, Mr. Tom by Michelle Magorian through a care-centered framework, arguing that the novel constructs care as a reciprocal process that reshapes both children and adults. Set during the Second World War, the narrative follows William Beech, a neglected evacuee from London, whose recovery is not only supported by Tom Oakley, his psychological parent, but also by the wider communal life of Little Weirwold. Through his interactions with adults, peers, and the village community, William acquires emotional stability, autonomy, and a sense of belonging. In particular, Zach, another evacuee boy, offers a form of empathy and guidance that Tom cannot provide, enabling William to confront internalized fear and shame regarding sexuality and to begin developing independent thought. At the same time, William’s arrival catalyzes Tom’s own process of emotional recovery. Having long suppressed the deaths of his wife Rachel and infant son, Tom is drawn back into memory, creativity, and social connection through caring for William. Critical Reflections on Biographical Representations of Scientists in Award-Winning Science, Technology, Engineering, and Math Books
abstract: Abstract Children’s early encounters with narrative nonfiction shape their developing understandings of who belongs in scientific spaces. While representation of women and racially minoritized people in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) fields remains uneven, less attention has been paid to the representational landscape of the books educators rely upon to introduce young learners to scientists. Drawing on a critical content analysis of 234 biographies and field profiles included on the National Science Teachers Association’s Outstanding Science Trade Books lists (1996–2024), we examined patterns of gender and racial representation and the ways structural barriers are narrated. Findings revealed persistent racial underrepresentation, uneven progress in gender representation, and a patterned tendency for injustice to be narrated primarily in the lives of those excluded from power. We argue that award-sanctioned STEM biographies both expand and constrain possibilities for children’s STEM identity development. title: IRL Tragedy, AI Comfort: Bereavement, Griefbots, and the Ethics of Thanatechnology in Dante Medema’s Message Not Found
abstract: Abstract The impact of generative AI on the lives of young people has been the subject of extensive discussion, and most of it has been negative. Dante Medema’s young adult novel Message Not Found does not join the existing chorus of voices lamenting, fearing, and denouncing AI; rather, it offers a compelling portrait of how this new technology can be a resource, asset, and even lifeline for young adults. Message Not Found follows Bailey Pierce, a high school senior in rural Alaska who, after her best friend Vanessa dies in a car accident, creates an AI chatbot to mimic her. The digital avatar is the source of comfort and companionship for the bereft narrator-protagonist. At the same time, it is also a vehicle for growth and insight. Bailey’s exchanges with the griefbot include unsettling conversations, shocking realizations, and even terrible truths. By the end of the novel, Bailey’s negative experiences with AI technology prove to be as valuable as the positive ones, and perhaps more so. In so doing, Message Not Found offers a more nuanced, complicated, and measured view of machine learning—and, ironically, of what it means to be human.

Dystopian Children’s Literature in Socialist and Post-socialist Contexts: The Case of Auto-Moto Ants
abstract: Abstract Young adult and children’s dystopias enable young readers to engage with social structures and their contradictions; as these are culturally specific, dystopia may be understood as culturally contingent, which suggests the need to expand critical discussions that have largely centred on the anglophone production of this genre. This article focuses on dystopia within socialist and post-socialist contexts. During the Cold War, children’s literature, particularly fantasy narratives, provided Eastern European authors with a medium for articulating veiled political critiques. Jože Snoj's Auto-Moto Ants (1975) provides an interesting illustration of Hunt’s (2009) claim that the best children’s literature preserves traditional structures while subtly undermining them, since it hyperbolically subverts socialist ideology in the dystopian world and contrasts it with a nostalgic patriarchal family idyll in the primary world. The representation of technology further intensifies this subversive-conservative ambivalence, functioning both as an instrument of control over the auto-moto ant collective and as a means of empowerment and liberation for the child protagonists. “A is for Bee”: Aesthetic Orchestration in Multilingual Picturebooks
abstract: Abstract Contemporary multilingual picturebooks combine languages with visual systems in ways that move beyond simple juxtaposition, yet research has largely approached these texts through reader-response theory or pedagogical utility rather than as artistic innovations. We introduce the Aesthetic Orchestration Framework (AOF), which operationalises multimodal semiotic orchestration through five analytical dimensions: artistic technique and visual design, typography and graphical elements, creative integration of linguistic resources, affective and sensory dimensions, and narrative structure and reading pathways. Applying the AOF through collaborative autoethnography, we examine how Ellen Heck, Sam Winston, and Shaun Tan create aesthetic experiences through deliberate compositional choices in three contemporary multilingual picturebooks. Our analysis reveals consistent orchestration principles across these works: refusing linguistic hierarchies through equal visual treatment, generating productive disorientation that activates metalinguistic awareness, creating affective fields through formal choices, and using aesthetic means to carry political arguments. title: Metafiction and Narrative Hierarchy in Postmodern Children’s Literature: The Cases of The Monster at the End of This Book and The Bear Who Wasn’t There
abstract: Abstract This study aims to examine the function of metafiction techniques in children’s literature and their impact on the reader’s world of meaning through the books The Monster at the End of This Book and The Bear Who Wasn’t There . The sample of the research is selected from study that concretize the interaction between the reader and the character levels through the act of “turning pages.” In The Monster at the End of This Book , the character Grover warns the reader not to turn the pages and attempts to halt the narrative’s progression through physical barriers like tying the pages with rope, nailing them, and building a wall. In The Bear Who Wasn’t There, on the other hand, due to the physical absence of the main character and the deliberate creation of gaps in the narrative, the secondary characters encourage the reader to continue turning the pages . These different forms of guidance in the works show that the reader’s physical intervention becomes a constitutive element of the narrative. “You’re the Connection”: Surfacing Marginalized Histories and Constructing Belonging in Maizy Chen’s Last Chance
abstract: Abstract This study applies Asian Critical Theory to conduct a content analysis of the middle-grade novel Maizy Chen’s Last Chance . Guided by three key tenets, Asianization, transnational contexts, and (re)constructive history, we examine how the novel disrupts racialized stereotypes, challenges the perpetual foreigner narrative, and recovers marginalized episodes of Chinese American history. Findings center on three thematic insights. First, the novel’s portrayal of the forever foreigner stereotype shows how Chinese Americans, regardless of birthplace or citizenship, are repeatedly positioned as outsiders through racialized rhetoric, underscoring the persistence of Asianization. Second, the novel highlights the contrast between first-generation immigrants’ deep ties to their homeland and later generations’ more distant connections, illustrating the complexity of diaspora identities within transnational contexts. Third, Lucky’s migration from Guangdong to San Francisco to Minnesota demonstrates how multi-generational storytelling restores neglected histories, fulfilling the aims of (re)constructive history. Reading Without Words: Sensory Inclusion and Meaning-Making in Children’s Multimodal Texts
abstract: Abstract In today’s diversified learning environments, children encounter an expanding range of multimodal texts that integrate image, sound, movement, and gesture. Such texts invite new forms of engagement and demand approaches that recognise the sensory as central to literacy learning. This article examines how ten wordless animated short films from the DIALLS project might communicate equity, inclusion, and ethical meaning through sensory and multimodal design. Drawing on critical sensory multimodal literacy and the kineikonic mode, a framework for analysing how image, movement, and sound interact in film, the study interprets these multimodal artefacts as ethical texts that perform, rather than declare, social values. Through close analysis of sound, rhythm, colour, and gesture, the films are shown to translate moral ideas such as fairness, cooperation, and care into sensory and affective forms. This sensory orchestration transforms abstract concepts into embodied experiences, positioning emotion as a precursor to ethical reflection.
